title: The AI That Solved Biology's 50-Year Puzzle
sentences: For fifty years, scientists struggled to predict the shape of a single protein.
Then an AI called AlphaFold started doing it in minutes.
Proteins are tiny machines inside your body, and their shape decides what they do.
Figuring out one shape used to take a lab years of work.
AlphaFold has now predicted structures for hundreds of millions of proteins.
Its creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Researchers now use it to design new medicines and enzymes faster than ever.
Follow for more tech that is quietly changing the future.

title: Why Your Next Phone Battery Could Be Solid
sentences: Your phone battery has a liquid inside it, and that liquid is the problem.
Today's lithium-ion batteries use a flammable liquid electrolyte.
Solid-state batteries replace it with a solid material.
That could mean more energy in the same space and a much lower fire risk.
Car makers are racing to build them for electric vehicles that charge faster and drive further.
The hard part is making them cheaply and keeping them stable for thousands of charges.
If engineers crack it, range anxiety could become history.
Follow for more future tech explained in under a minute.

title: People Are Controlling Computers With Their Thoughts
sentences: Some people are now moving a cursor using only their thoughts.
It works with a brain-computer interface, a tiny device that reads signals from neurons.
When you imagine moving your hand, your brain fires a pattern.
AI software learns that pattern and turns it into a click or a typed letter.
In clinical trials, people with paralysis have used these implants to text, browse and even play games.
Researchers have also turned brain signals into speech for people who lost their voice.
It is still early and experimental, but the results are stunning.
Follow for more inventions that sound like science fiction.

title: The Day Fusion Made More Energy Than It Used
sentences: In December 2022, scientists did something they had chased for seventy years.
At the National Ignition Facility in California, a fusion reaction released more energy than the lasers put into it.
Fusion is how the Sun makes power: smashing light atoms together.
It produces no carbon and very little long-lived waste.
The catch is that the whole facility still used far more electricity than it produced.
Dozens of companies are now trying to turn this into real power plants.
If they succeed, it could change energy forever.
Follow to see where fusion goes next.

title: Meat Grown Without Animals
sentences: What if your burger never came from a farm animal?
Cultivated meat is grown from a small sample of animal cells.
The cells are fed nutrients in steel tanks, similar to brewing beer.
They multiply into real muscle and fat tissue.
Singapore became the first country to approve it for sale, and the United States followed with cultivated chicken.
The big challenges are cost and scaling up to millions of meals.
Supporters say it could use far less land and water than traditional farming.
Follow for more food tech from the future.

title: The Crystal That Could Beat Silicon Solar Panels
sentences: A strange crystal could make solar panels cheaper and more powerful.
It is called perovskite, and it can be printed almost like ink.
In labs, perovskite cells improved faster than almost any solar technology in history.
Stacked on top of silicon, these tandem cells have broken efficiency records.
The problem is that perovskites can break down from heat and moisture.
Companies are now testing tougher versions on real rooftops.
If they last, solar power could get a huge upgrade.
Follow for more clean energy breakthroughs.

title: Why Quantum Computers Are So Hard to Build
sentences: Quantum computers could solve problems that would take normal computers longer than the age of the universe.
Instead of bits that are zero or one, they use qubits that can be both at once.
But qubits are incredibly fragile.
Heat, vibration or a stray signal can ruin a calculation in a split second.
That is why many quantum chips are cooled colder than outer space.
The big race now is error correction, combining many shaky qubits into one reliable one.
Recent experiments suggest that this approach can actually work.
Follow to keep up with the quantum race.

title: AI Is Now Writing Code for Programmers
sentences: A huge amount of new software is now written with help from AI.
Coding assistants can suggest whole functions as a programmer types.
Newer AI agents can read a codebase, fix bugs and run tests on their own.
They learned by studying enormous amounts of public code.
But they still make mistakes, so humans need to review what they write.
Many developers say the job is shifting from typing code to directing and checking it.
The skill that matters most might be knowing what to build.
Follow for more on how AI is changing work.

title: Riding in a Car With No Driver
sentences: In some cities, you can already hail a car with nobody in the driver's seat.
Robotaxis use cameras, radar and spinning laser sensors called lidar to see the road.
AI combines all that data to predict what every car, cyclist and pedestrian will do next.
Companies like Waymo now run fully driverless rides in several American cities.
They still struggle with rare situations, bad weather and confusing road works.
The question is no longer if they work, but how fast they can spread safely.
Would you ride in one?
Follow for more future transport.

title: Beaming Solar Power From Space
sentences: What if solar panels in space could beam electricity down to Earth?
In orbit, the Sun never sets and there are no clouds.
A space solar station would collect sunlight and send it down as microwaves.
A large antenna on the ground would turn those microwaves back into electricity.
In 2023, a Caltech experiment beamed a small amount of power from space for the first time.
Building a full-size station would require huge structures and cheap rocket launches.
It sounds wild, but several space agencies are seriously studying it.
Follow for more ideas that could power the future.

title: The First Approved CRISPR Cure
sentences: Doctors can now edit a patient's DNA to treat a serious disease.
In 2023, regulators approved the first CRISPR-based therapy, for sickle cell disease.
Sickle cell makes red blood cells bend into a sickle shape, causing severe pain.
The treatment edits a patient's own stem cells so their body makes healthier blood.
Many patients in trials stopped having painful crises.
It is extremely expensive and complex for now.
But it proves gene editing has moved from the lab to the clinic.
Follow for more medical tech breakthroughs.

title: Humanoid Robots Are Getting Jobs
sentences: Robots shaped like humans are starting to show up in factories and warehouses.
Why build a robot with arms and legs?
Because our world is designed for human bodies: stairs, shelves, doors and tools.
A humanoid could, in theory, work anywhere a person can.
AI is helping these robots learn tasks by watching examples instead of being programmed step by step.
Right now they are slow, expensive and mostly in pilot programs.
But many companies are betting billions that this will change.
Follow for more on the robot revolution.

title: Pulling Drinking Water Out of Thin Air
sentences: Even desert air contains water, and scientists have found ways to catch it.
Special materials called metal-organic frameworks act like microscopic sponges.
At night, they soak up water vapor from the air.
During the day, sunlight warms them and releases the water to be collected.
The scientists who developed these materials won the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Devices like this are still small, but they work with no electricity grid.
One day they could help places where clean water is scarce.
Follow for more inventions solving real problems.

title: How to Spot a Deepfake
sentences: Deepfakes are AI videos that make people appear to say things they never said.
They are getting harder to spot every month.
Old tricks like weird blinking no longer work reliably.
The best defense is checking the source, not just the pixels.
Ask who posted it first, and whether trusted news outlets are reporting it.
Tech companies are also adding hidden labels and watermarks to AI-generated media.
When something feels designed to make you angry fast, pause before you share.
Follow for more ways to stay smart about AI.

title: AI Can Now Predict the Weather
sentences: Weather forecasts used to need some of the biggest supercomputers on Earth.
Now AI models can produce a ten-day forecast in about a minute.
Systems like Google DeepMind's GraphCast learned from decades of past weather data.
In tests, they matched or beat traditional forecasts on many measurements.
Weather agencies are now running AI models alongside their classic physics models.
The hope is earlier warnings for storms, floods and heatwaves.
The physics still matters, but AI is a powerful new tool.
Follow for more AI that actually helps.

title: Houses Printed by Giant Robots
sentences: Some new homes are not built brick by brick, they are printed.
A huge 3D printer squeezes out layers of special concrete, like icing on a cake.
The walls of a small house can be printed in a matter of days.
It can reduce waste and the number of workers needed on site.
Printed homes and even neighborhoods already exist in the United States, Europe and Mexico.
Roofs, wiring and plumbing are still mostly done the traditional way.
But this could help build homes faster and cheaper.
Follow for more future construction tech.

title: Farms That Grow Upward
sentences: Some farms do not have fields; they have shelves stacked to the ceiling.
Vertical farms grow crops indoors under LED lights.
Plants get exactly the water and nutrients they need, often with no soil at all.
That can use far less water and no pesticides, and crops grow year round.
The big problem is electricity, because lights and climate control are expensive.
Several vertical farming startups have struggled or shut down because of those costs.
Cheaper clean energy could decide whether this idea grows or fades.
Follow for more honest takes on future tech.

title: Glasses That Put a Screen in Front of Your Eyes
sentences: Your next screen might sit right in front of your eyes.
Smart glasses can show directions, messages and translations floating in your view.
Some include cameras and AI assistants that can describe what you are looking at.
The hard part is fitting a display, battery and computer into normal-looking frames.
Early versions were bulky, but each new generation gets lighter.
They also raise big privacy questions about cameras in public.
Many tech companies believe glasses could one day replace phones.
Follow for more on the future of screens.

title: Digital Twins: Copying the Real World Into Software
sentences: Engineers are building virtual copies of jet engines, factories and even whole cities.
These copies are called digital twins.
Sensors on the real object constantly feed data into the virtual one.
Engineers can test changes on the twin before touching the real thing.
Airlines use them to predict when an engine part needs replacing.
Cities use them to plan traffic and flood defenses.
Some researchers even want digital twins of the human heart to test treatments.
Follow for more tech that is shaping the future.

title: Machines That Suck Carbon Out of the Sky
sentences: There are machines that pull carbon dioxide straight out of the air.
It is called direct air capture.
Giant fans push air through filters that grab carbon dioxide.
The carbon can then be stored deep underground, where it turns into rock over time.
Plants like this already operate in Iceland and the United States.
Right now it is expensive and uses a lot of energy, and it captures only a tiny amount.
Experts say it can help, but cutting emissions still matters most.
Follow for more climate tech explained.

title: The Wonder Material Made From Pencil Lead
sentences: A material thinner than anything else was first isolated using sticky tape and pencil graphite.
It is called graphene, a sheet of carbon just one atom thick.
It is incredibly strong, flexible, and conducts electricity extremely well.
The scientists who isolated it won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010.
It is already used in some sports gear, coatings and batteries.
Making large, perfect sheets cheaply is still the big challenge.
Researchers dream of graphene chips, filters and super-strong materials.
Follow for more materials of the future.

title: Robotic Suits That Make You Stronger
sentences: Some workers are wearing robotic suits to lift heavy loads.
These are called exoskeletons.
Motors or springs support the back, shoulders or legs to reduce strain.
Factories use them so workers get less tired and injured.
In hospitals, powered exoskeletons help some people with spinal injuries stand and walk during therapy.
AI helps newer models predict how you want to move.
They are still pricey, but they are getting lighter and smarter.
Follow for more human upgrade tech.

title: mRNA Vaccines Might Fight Cancer Next
sentences: The technology behind some COVID vaccines is now being tested against cancer.
mRNA works like a set of instructions that teaches your cells to make a target protein.
For cancer, scientists read the mutations in a patient's tumor.
Then they design a personalized mRNA vaccine to train the immune system to attack it.
Early clinical trials, especially in melanoma, have shown encouraging results.
Larger trials are needed before these become standard treatments.
If they work, cancer care could become truly personal.
Follow for more medical breakthroughs.

title: Why the Hyperloop Never Happened
sentences: The Hyperloop promised pods racing through tubes faster than a plane.
The idea was to remove most of the air from a tube, so pods could glide with very little drag.
Billions of dollars and huge hype followed.
But keeping hundreds of kilometers of tube near vacuum is brutally hard and expensive.
Safety, land costs and passenger comfort were also giant problems.
One of the most famous Hyperloop companies shut down in 2023.
It is a reminder that a cool demo is not the same as a working system.
Follow for honest stories about future tech.

title: Flying Taxis Are Almost Here
sentences: Air taxis that take off like helicopters but sound much quieter are being tested right now.
They are called eVTOLs, electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft.
Many use several small electric rotors instead of one big noisy one.
The goal is short city hops, like airport to downtown in minutes.
Companies are working through strict aviation safety certification.
Battery weight still limits how far and how many passengers they can carry.
The first commercial routes may start in a few cities soon.
Follow for more future transport.

title: Computer Chips That Work Like a Brain
sentences: Your brain runs on about the power of a dim light bulb, and computers are jealous.
Neuromorphic chips try to copy how the brain works.
Instead of constant processing, their artificial neurons fire only when something changes.
That can make some AI tasks use far less energy.
Intel, IBM and university labs have built experimental neuromorphic chips.
They could power smart sensors, robots and devices that run on tiny batteries.
As AI's energy use grows, ideas like this matter more.
Follow for more chip tech.

title: Storing the Internet in DNA
sentences: All of the world's data could, in theory, fit in a surprisingly small box of DNA.
DNA stores information using four letters, A, C, G and T.
Scientists can translate digital files into those letters and build matching DNA strands.
They have already stored books, images and even a short movie this way.
Stored cold and dry, DNA can survive for thousands of years.
Right now, writing and reading DNA is still slow and expensive.
But for long-term archives, it could be the ultimate hard drive.
Follow for more mind-bending tech.

title: A Battery Made of Sand
sentences: In Finland, a giant tank of sand stores energy to heat homes.
It is called a sand battery.
Cheap electricity from wind and solar heats the sand to hundreds of degrees.
Sand holds that heat for a long time, inside an insulated silo.
When homes need warmth, the stored heat flows into the local heating network.
It cannot easily turn heat back into electricity, but it is simple and cheap.
Sometimes the best future tech is surprisingly low tech.
Follow for more clever energy ideas.

title: Using AI to Understand Whales
sentences: Scientists are using AI to try to understand how sperm whales communicate.
Sperm whales talk in patterns of clicks called codas.
Project CETI records thousands of these clicks with underwater microphones.
AI looks for structure, like which patterns repeat in which situations.
Researchers have found that whale codas are more complex than once thought.
We are still far from a whale-to-English translator.
But AI is giving us our best chance yet to listen.
Follow for more AI meets nature.

title: Rockets That Land Themselves
sentences: Rockets used to be thrown away after a single launch.
Now some boosters fly back and land upright, ready to fly again.
SpaceX's Falcon 9 boosters have flown many missions each.
Reusing rockets has helped cut the cost of reaching orbit.
Starship aims to make the entire rocket reusable, and its booster has even been caught by the launch tower's mechanical arms.
Cheap launches could make space stations, satellites and Moon missions far more common.
We may be at the start of a new space age.
Follow for more space tech.

title: Diamonds Made in a Lab
sentences: Many diamonds sold today were grown in a lab, not dug from the ground.
Lab-grown diamonds are real diamonds, made of the same carbon crystal.
One method recreates the crushing heat and pressure deep inside the Earth.
Another builds diamonds layer by layer from a carbon-rich gas.
Even experts need special machines to tell them apart from mined stones.
Diamonds are also amazing for tech, from cutting tools to quantum sensors.
The future of diamonds may be in electronics, not just jewelry.
Follow for more surprising science.

title: Concrete That Heals Its Own Cracks
sentences: Engineers have made concrete that can repair its own cracks.
The secret is bacteria mixed into the concrete, along with their food.
The bacteria stay dormant for years.
When a crack lets in water, they wake up and produce limestone that seals the gap.
Small cracks can close on their own, without a repair crew.
This could make bridges, tunnels and buildings last longer.
Concrete production is also a major source of emissions, so lasting longer matters.
Follow for more futuristic materials.

title: Roads That Charge Your Car While You Drive
sentences: Imagine charging your electric car just by driving down the road.
Some test roads have coils buried under the surface.
They create a magnetic field that sends power to a receiver under the car.
This is the same idea as wireless phone charging, but much bigger.
Pilot projects are running in places like Sweden, Israel and the United States.
Cost is the big challenge, since roads would need to be dug up.
If it works, electric cars could carry smaller, cheaper batteries.
Follow for more future transport ideas.

title: Robots in the Operating Room
sentences: Millions of surgeries have already been done with help from robots.
In most cases, a human surgeon controls the robot from a console.
The robot holds tiny tools through small cuts and filters out hand tremors.
That can mean smaller scars and faster recovery for some procedures.
Researchers are now testing robots that can do some surgical steps on their own.
One experimental robot has performed parts of operations on animals autonomously.
For now, the surgeon is still firmly in charge.
Follow for more medical tech.

title: Implants That Restore Some Vision
sentences: Scientists are building devices to help some blind people see again.
Some retinal implants turn camera images into electrical pulses.
Those pulses stimulate the remaining cells in the eye.
The brain learns to read them as flashes and shapes of light.
Other projects send signals directly to the vision area of the brain.
The images are still very basic, far from normal sight.
But even seeing doorways and shapes can change a life.
Follow for more tech that helps people.

title: Mining Asteroids for Treasure
sentences: Some asteroids may contain huge amounts of valuable metals.
Companies dream of mining them for platinum, nickel and water.
Water may be the real prize, because it can be turned into rocket fuel in space.
NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission already brought a sample of an asteroid back to Earth.
Japan's Hayabusa missions did it too.
But real mining would need robots that work far from home for years.
It is decades away, but the first steps have happened.
Follow for more space ideas.

title: How ChatGPT Actually Works
sentences: Chatbots like ChatGPT do not look up answers the way a search engine does.
They are large language models trained to predict the next word.
During training, they read huge amounts of text and learn patterns in language.
When you ask a question, they generate an answer one small piece at a time.
Extra training with human feedback teaches them to be more helpful.
That is why they can sound confident even when they are wrong.
Understanding this makes you a smarter AI user.
Follow for more AI explained simply.

title: Why AI Makes Things Up
sentences: AI chatbots sometimes invent facts, quotes or even fake sources.
This is called a hallucination.
It happens because the model generates words that sound likely, not words it has checked.
If it lacks the real answer, it can still produce something that sounds right.
Newer systems reduce this by searching the web or citing documents.
But no chatbot is perfect.
For anything important, check a reliable source.
Follow for more tips on using AI wisely.

title: Chips So Small They Are Measured in Atoms
sentences: The chip in your phone has billions of transistors, each almost unimaginably tiny.
For decades, the number of transistors on chips doubled about every two years.
That trend is called Moore's Law.
Now features are so small that engineers fight the laws of physics itself.
Machines using extreme ultraviolet light are needed to print these patterns.
Chip makers are also stacking chips in 3D to keep improving.
The race for smaller chips powers everything from phones to AI.
Follow for more chip tech.

title: Nuclear Reactors Small Enough to Ship
sentences: The next nuclear power plant might be built in a factory and delivered by truck.
They are called small modular reactors.
Instead of one giant custom project, factories could build standard units.
That could make them faster to build and easier to place near cities or data centers.
Many designs use passive safety that cools the reactor without pumps.
Several are in development, but costs and approvals are still big hurdles.
Tech companies are interested because AI needs a lot of power.
Follow for more energy tech.

title: Enzymes That Eat Plastic
sentences: Scientists have found tiny proteins that can break down plastic.
In 2016, researchers in Japan found bacteria at a recycling site that could digest PET plastic.
PET is the plastic used in many drink bottles.
Scientists then engineered faster versions of the enzyme those bacteria used.
Some can break plastic back into building blocks to make new plastic.
Companies are now testing this kind of recycling on an industrial scale.
It will not solve plastic pollution alone, but it could help.
Follow for more green tech.

title: Real Holograms Are Coming
sentences: Science fiction holograms are getting closer to reality.
Most so-called holograms on stage are actually clever reflections.
Light field displays send different images to each eye, so you see real depth.
Some can show 3D images that many people can view at once, without glasses.
Researchers are also using AI to calculate holograms faster.
The big challenge is the massive amount of computing they need.
One day, video calls could feel like the person is in the room.
Follow for more future displays.

title: AI Running Inside Your Phone
sentences: More and more AI now runs directly on your phone, not in the cloud.
New chips include special units designed just for AI math.
That lets phones translate, edit photos and summarize text without sending everything online.
On-device AI can be faster and more private.
The trade-off is that phones have less power than giant data centers.
So companies shrink AI models to fit inside your pocket.
Your next phone upgrade might be mostly an AI upgrade.
Follow for more AI tech.

title: Pig Kidneys in Human Patients
sentences: Doctors have transplanted kidneys from pigs into living people.
There are not nearly enough human organs for everyone who needs one.
So scientists gene-edit pigs to make their organs less likely to be rejected.
They also remove pig viruses that could be risky.
The first transplant of a gene-edited pig kidney into a living patient happened in 2024.
Results have been mixed, but each case teaches doctors more.
This could one day shorten organ waiting lists.
Follow for more medical frontiers.

title: Machines Cleaning the Ocean
sentences: Huge floating systems are pulling plastic out of the ocean.
Ocean currents gather plastic in giant swirling zones.
The Ocean Cleanup uses long floating barriers, towed by boats, to collect it.
They also place barriers in rivers to stop plastic before it reaches the sea.
The collected plastic is brought to shore for recycling.
Critics say we still need to stop plastic at the source.
But cleanup tech is getting better every year.
Follow for more climate and ocean tech.

title: Making Oxygen on Mars
sentences: A gadget the size of a lunchbox made oxygen on Mars.
It was called MOXIE and it rode on NASA's Perseverance rover.
Mars air is mostly carbon dioxide.
MOXIE split carbon dioxide molecules to release oxygen.
Over several runs, it proved the idea works on another planet.
Future machines would need to be much bigger to support astronauts.
Making air and fuel on Mars could make human missions possible.
Follow for more space tech.

title: AI Is Designing New Medicines
sentences: Developing a new drug can take over ten years and billions of dollars.
AI is trying to speed that up.
Models can scan millions of possible molecules and predict which ones might work.
Others help design entirely new proteins that do not exist in nature.
Several AI-discovered drug candidates are now being tested in clinical trials.
But every drug still has to prove it is safe and effective in people.
AI might not replace scientists, but it can point them in the right direction faster.
Follow for more AI in medicine.

title: Internet From Thousands of Satellites
sentences: Thousands of satellites now beam internet down to Earth.
Old satellite internet used a few satellites very far away, which made it slow to respond.
New networks like Starlink use satellites in low orbit, much closer to us.
That makes the connection fast enough for video calls and gaming.
It is bringing internet to remote villages, ships and planes.
Astronomers worry about the bright streaks these satellites leave in telescope images.
Space is getting crowded, fast.
Follow for more space and internet tech.

title: Paying With the Palm of Your Hand
sentences: In some stores, you can now pay by simply hovering your hand.
Palm scanners read the unique pattern of lines and veins in your palm.
Vein patterns are under the skin, which makes them hard to fake.
Your palm is linked to a payment card, so no phone or wallet is needed.
Supporters say it is fast and convenient.
Privacy experts warn that biometric data cannot be changed if it ever leaks.
Would you trust your hand as your wallet?
Follow for more future tech.

title: Computers Built From Brain Cells
sentences: Researchers are wiring living brain cells to computer chips.
They grow tiny clusters of human neurons called brain organoids.
In one experiment, a dish of neurons learned to play a simple version of the video game Pong.
Scientists hope living neurons could one day compute using very little energy.
This field is sometimes called organoid intelligence.
It also raises serious ethical questions that scientists are actively debating.
It is early, strange and fascinating.
Follow for more frontier science.

title: The Superconductor Hype That Fooled the Internet
sentences: In 2023, the internet went wild over a material called LK-99.
Its creators claimed it was a superconductor at room temperature.
A superconductor carries electricity with zero resistance and almost no energy loss.
A room-temperature version could transform power grids, computers and transport.
Labs around the world raced to copy it within weeks.
Their results showed that LK-99 was not a superconductor after all.
Science worked exactly as it should: test, check and correct.
Follow for honest tech stories.

title: Robot Dogs Are Doing Real Jobs
sentences: Four-legged robots are now inspecting factories, power plants and construction sites.
Legs let them climb stairs and cross rough ground where wheels get stuck.
Robots like Boston Dynamics' Spot carry cameras and sensors on their backs.
They can patrol the same route every day and spot leaks, heat or damage.
That keeps humans out of dangerous places.
AI is teaching newer robots to walk by practicing millions of times in simulation.
The robot dog has gone from viral video to coworker.
Follow for more robotics.

title: AI Can Now Make Music
sentences: You can now type a sentence and get a full song back from an AI.
Music models learn patterns of melody, rhythm and sound from huge audio collections.
Some can generate vocals, lyrics and instruments in seconds.
Musicians use them to brainstorm ideas and demos.
Record labels and artists are fighting in court over what music these models trained on.
The big question is who owns a song an AI helped create.
Music is entering a whole new era.
Follow for more AI culture.

title: Windows That Make Electricity
sentences: What if every window in a skyscraper was also a solar panel?
Transparent solar cells let visible light pass through while capturing invisible light.
They mostly absorb ultraviolet and infrared light that our eyes cannot see.
That means a window can look almost normal and still make power.
They are less efficient than regular solar panels.
But cities have huge amounts of glass, so it could add up.
Buildings could start powering themselves.
Follow for more clean energy ideas.

title: Planes That Run on Hydrogen
sentences: Aviation is one of the hardest industries to make climate friendly.
One idea is to fly planes on hydrogen.
Hydrogen can power fuel cells that drive electric motors, or be burned in special engines.
Either way, the main exhaust is water vapor.
The problem is that hydrogen takes up a lot of space and must be stored very cold.
Small test planes have already flown on hydrogen power.
Big passenger jets running on it are still many years away.
Follow for more future aviation.

title: Prosthetic Hands That Can Feel
sentences: Some prosthetic hands can now send a sense of touch back to the user.
Sensors in the fingertips measure pressure.
Those signals are sent to nerves in the remaining arm.
The brain feels it as touch, as if it came from a real hand.
In studies, users could handle delicate objects like eggs or grapes more easily.
AI helps decode muscle signals so the hand moves more naturally.
The goal is a prosthetic that feels like part of your body.
Follow for more human-tech breakthroughs.

title: Humans Are Going Back to the Moon
sentences: For the first time in over fifty years, humans are preparing to return to the Moon.
NASA's Artemis program aims to land astronauts near the lunar south pole.
That region may hold water ice in permanently shadowed craters.
Ice could provide drinking water, oxygen and even rocket fuel.
The plan includes a small space station orbiting the Moon.
Several countries, and private companies, are sending landers too.
The Moon could become a stepping stone to Mars.
Follow for more space news.

title: AI Agents That Do Tasks for You
sentences: The next step for AI is not just answering questions, but doing tasks.
AI agents can browse websites, fill forms and use apps on your behalf.
You could ask one to research flights or organize your files.
They work by planning steps, taking an action, then checking the result.
Right now, they still get confused and need supervision.
Security is a big concern, because an agent with access to your accounts must be trusted.
Expect AI that acts, not just talks.
Follow for more AI updates.

title: Will AI Take Your Job?
sentences: Will AI take your job?
The honest answer is that it will change many jobs more than it erases them.
AI is very good at repetitive tasks with clear patterns.
It is weaker at real-world judgment, physical skill and human trust.
Some roles will shrink, and new roles will appear, as happened with computers and the internet.
People who learn to work with AI tools often get the biggest advantage.
The best move is to stay curious and keep learning.
Follow for more on the future of work.

title: Batteries That Store the Sun for Night
sentences: Solar power has one obvious problem: the Sun goes down.
Giant battery farms are now storing daytime solar energy for the evening.
When demand peaks after sunset, the batteries release power to the grid.
Battery prices have dropped dramatically over the past decade.
Places like California now regularly run on large amounts of stored solar power at night.
Researchers are also testing cheaper chemistries, like sodium and iron, instead of lithium.
Storage is the missing piece of a clean grid.
Follow for more energy tech.

title: Tiny Robots That Could Swim Inside You
sentences: Scientists are building robots small enough to travel inside the body.
Some are guided with magnets from outside the body.
Researchers hope they could deliver medicine exactly where it is needed.
Others are made of soft materials that dissolve after their job is done.
So far, most tests have been in the lab and in animals.
Controlling something so tiny inside a moving body is very hard.
But the idea of a robot doctor in your bloodstream is getting closer.
Follow for more future medicine.

title: The Telescope Looking Back in Time
sentences: The James Webb Space Telescope is a time machine.
Light from distant galaxies takes billions of years to reach us.
So Webb sees those galaxies as they were long ago.
It observes in infrared light, which can pass through cosmic dust.
Webb has spotted some of the earliest galaxies ever seen.
It can even study the air of planets orbiting other stars.
Every new image is a postcard from the early universe.
Follow for more space discoveries.
